```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Time to first payment fits the 90-day goal better for A. A charges a small self-serve subscription (anchored to ReviewGuard's published $1.99/month Pro tier), so one paying user can arrive soon after launch. B's main revenue is a closing fee on a startup sale, which needs a buyer and a seller to find each other, do due diligence, and close through escrow. Neither brief gives any cycle-length data suggesting that fits inside 90 days.",
    "B has documented cold-start trouble. The closest comparable (DealMyApp) reports weak buyer conversion two weeks in. A $750 Indie Hackers newsletter test aimed at a similar audience produced 124 clicks and zero sales. A two-sided marketplace needs liquidity on both sides before anyone pays, and that is much harder for one operator.",
    "A is simpler to set up and run. It needs no escrow vendor, no state-by-state broker-licensing check, and no handling of sensitive financial or identity data. B lists all three, and its data-handling obligation is explicitly flagged as unsourced. A's on-device scoring also avoids ongoing inference costs.",
    "A has a near-zero-cost distribution path: vocal, self-organizing subreddits plus a Product Hunt or HN launch, with a cited benchmark of about 1,000 installs in a week for a strong launch. A's demand evidence also includes platform-level acknowledgment of the problem (the Reddit CEO via an FT report summarized by Slashdot), not just individual complaints.",
    "Both ideas face saturated markets: A has four free competitors and B has five, three of them at 0% or near-0% commission. Competition therefore does not separate them. The deciding factors are speed to first revenue and operational burden, and both favor A."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence is the thinnest part of its brief. It consists of one anecdotal seller quote (\"I didn't know where serious buyers were\") and a self-reported traffic figure from a competing marketplace's own operator two weeks after launch. Neither shows anyone paying. The second quote actually undercuts demand on the buyer side, which is the side that determines whether deals close and fees get collected.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A's willingness-to-pay is essentially unproven. The only price anchor is one competitor's published $1.99/month tier, with no install, conversion, or revenue data from any competitor. Four free, maintained alternatives also make paid conversion doubtful. A also carries false-positive and platform-ToS risk. A wins mainly because B's documented failure modes (buyer liquidity, a zero-sale paid test, slow closing-fee revenue, escrow and licensing setup) are worse obstacles to a paying customer within 90 days, not because A's case is strong on its own."
}
```
